subject: mathematics
question_text: Show that the points (5, −1, 1), (7, −4, 7), (1, −6, 10) and (−1, −3, 4) are the vertices of a rhombus.

mark_split.label: Show all four sides are equal
Find the diagonals and show they differ

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.60 — SAQ chapter 8 Addition of Vectors, answer 53. Printed appearances: the single tag 'IPE 13' — a PRE-BIFURCATION paper, before the 2014 TS/AP split. appearances[].board has no value for that era, so the year is recorded here in prose and appearances[] is left empty rather than guessing a board. A rhombus needs BOTH halves: four equal sides AND unequal diagonals. Four equal sides alone would also fit a square, which is why the diagonals are checked. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed anywhere in this chapter. It follows the split the same book prints for the one 4-mark answer that does carry tags, Matrices answer 40 on book p.51. The book's chapter header carries ★★★ and reads '4 Marks'; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B runs Q11-Q17 at 4 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q12 is the Addition of Vectors slot. NOTE: Addition of Vectors has NO Section-C slot on the paper and no LAQ chapter in this book — the unit is SAQ and VSAQ only.

recall_prompt: Say how you would show four points make a rhombus — say everything you have to check.

steps.label: Find the side vectors
steps.margin_note: First mark. Take the points in the order given as A, B, C, D and go round: AB, BC, CD, DA. Order matters — a different order makes the same four points into a crossed shape.

recall.must_convey: That the four points are named A, B, C, D in the given order and the four side vectors AB, BC, CD, DA are found by subtraction.
accept: name them A B C D in order and find AB BC CD and DA by subtracting position vectors
go round the quadrilateral taking the four side vectors
find the four sides in order
naalugu points ni A B C D ani peru petti, naalugu sides kanukovali
work out the four side vectors in sequence

steps.why: A quadrilateral is only defined once the order of its vertices is fixed. Going round in the given order is what makes AB and CD opposite sides rather than crossing ones.
common_mistakes: Taking the points in a different order and getting a crossed figure.
Computing only two sides and assuming the rest.

steps.label: Draw the rhombus
steps.margin_note: Worth no mark but worth drawing. The four tick marks say all four SIDES are equal; the two dashed diagonals are what must come out UNEQUAL. Equal sides alone would allow a square, so both halves of the check are in the picture.

recall.must_convey: That rhombus ABCD is sketched with its four equal sides marked and both diagonals drawn. Naming the drawing is full credit — it cannot be spoken.
accept: draw the rhombus with all four sides equal and both diagonals
sketch A B C D with tick marks on the sides and the diagonals crossing
show the four equal sides and the two unequal diagonals
rhombus geesi naalugu sides equal ani mark chesi diagonals geeyali
draw the rhombus with its diagonals

steps.why: A rhombus needs BOTH facts: four equal sides, and diagonals that are not equal. Four equal sides on their own describe a square just as well, so the diagonals are what rule it out.
common_mistakes: Checking only that the four sides are equal, which a square also satisfies.
Taking AB and CD as diagonals — they are opposite sides.

steps.label: Show the sides are equal
steps.margin_note: Second mark. All four magnitudes come to 7 — and 4 + 9 + 36 = 49 every time, just with the numbers in a different order. Write all four out; three plus an assumption is not a proof.
lines: ∴ |AB| = |BC| = |CD| = |DA|, so all four sides are equal.

recall.must_convey: That all four side magnitudes are computed and each comes to 7, so the four sides are equal.
accept: all four magnitudes come to seven so the sides are equal
each side has length seven, root of forty nine
compute the four lengths and they are all seven
naalugu sides magnitude seven vasthundi, anni equal
the four sides are all equal in length

steps.why: Four equal sides is what makes a quadrilateral a rhombus OR a square. It is necessary but not yet sufficient, which is why the next step exists.
common_mistakes: Checking two sides and asserting the other two by symmetry.
Stopping here and calling it a rhombus.

steps.label: Check the diagonals
steps.margin_note: Third mark, and the half students skip. The diagonals are AC and BD — corner to opposite corner, not side to side. They must come out UNEQUAL, or the figure is a square.

recall.must_convey: That the diagonals AC and BD are found and their magnitudes, √122 and √74, are different.
accept: find the diagonals AC and BD, they come to root one twenty two and root seventy four which are unequal
the two diagonals have different lengths so it is not a square
check AC and BD and they are not equal
diagonals AC BD kanukunte root 122 and root 74, equal kaadu
the diagonals are unequal

steps.why: A square is a rhombus with equal diagonals. Showing they differ is what rules the square out and pins the figure down as a rhombus specifically.
common_mistakes: Taking AB and CD as the diagonals; those are sides.
Finding the diagonals but never comparing them.

steps.label: Conclude rhombus
steps.margin_note: Last mark. State both findings together — equal sides and unequal diagonals — because it is the pair of them that names the shape.
lines: All four sides are equal and the diagonals are unequal.

lines.text: ∴ A, B, C, D form a rhombus.

recall.must_convey: That four equal sides together with unequal diagonals makes the figure a rhombus.
accept: four equal sides and unequal diagonals so it is a rhombus
since the sides are equal but the diagonals are not, the figure is a rhombus
the four points form a rhombus
sides equal, diagonals equal kaadu, kabatti rhombus
therefore it is a rhombus and not a square

steps.why: Naming both conditions is what separates a rhombus from a square in the examiner’s eyes. One without the other does not identify the shape.
common_mistakes: Concluding rhombus from the equal sides alone.
Writing "hence proved" with neither condition named.
